title: The One Where Rachel Has A Baby (2)

jokes.text: This isn't some girl you picked up in a bar and humped.
jokes.setup: Ross's mom is making a sentimental case for giving Rachel the engagement ring
jokes.punchline: She undermines her own sentimental moment with the blunt, undignified word 'humped'
jokes.explanation: The comedy comes from the jarring tonal collision — a dignified maternal speech punctuated by the word 'humped.' Economy is the main strength here; one unexpected word does all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: How are you feeling?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: How am I feeling? Like someone's ripping out my internal organs through my pelvis with a claw hammer made of fire!

jokes.text: Joey (as Dr. Drake Ramoray) asking the woman: 'Do you sleep with women and never call them again?'
jokes.setup: Joey is pretending to be a doctor asking 'routine questions' to vet a man for Ross
jokes.punchline: The 'routine question' is transparently a personal interrogation about infidelity, completely breaking the doctor pretense
jokes.explanation: Very Joey — his inability to maintain a cover story and his loyal but ham-fisted attempt to help Ross. Character integration is high because only Joey would blow a cover this badly in this specific way.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: I'm pregnant!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh. My. God.

jokes.text: Should we tell Rachel there's an empty room right next to hers? / We could. Or we could have sex in it.
jokes.setup: Chandler asks a seemingly considerate question about telling Rachel about the empty room
jokes.punchline: Monica immediately pivots to using it for sex — revealing that's why they're bringing it up at all
jokes.explanation: Clean setup/punchline with good economy. The misdirection works — the audience expects a considerate offer, gets naked opportunism. Monica's bluntness is well-used.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, if you eat the gorilla, at least you can talk to it first and explain why you're eating it. With the dog, it just trusts you.

jokes.text: Let me think about that. While I remove my pants!
jokes.setup: Monica has suggested having sex in the hospital room
jokes.punchline: Chandler pre-emptively acts before 'thinking about it,' collapsing the deliberation joke
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of joke 3. The phrasing 'while I remove my pants' is the kind of deliberately awkward Chandler construction that made the character beloved. Not profound, but very functional.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That's very nice, Mon, but I'm not asking what you would do. I'm asking what a *normal* person would do.

jokes.text: Okay, mister! Fertilize me!
jokes.setup: Monica and Chandler are sneaking away to have sex in hopes of conceiving
jokes.punchline: Monica's clinical, commanding 'fertilize me' reduces romance to a reproductive transaction — very on-brand for obsessive Monica
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The character integration is exceptional — 'Fertilize me!' is Monica in two words: aggressive, goal-oriented, clinical even in romance. The word choice is both funny and deeply character-specific. Highly quotable, earns its laugh through characterization rather than shock.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I can't believe we're doing this.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Oh, come on, it'll be fun! Besides, you're the big spoon.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I feel more like a fork right now.

jokes.text: If it's not Janice, then there are two of them. And that would mean it's the end of the world!
jokes.setup: Someone hears a distinctive laugh/voice from the previously recapped episodes — suggesting Janice is in the hospital
jokes.punchline: Chandler's hyperbolic apocalyptic framing of Janice's presence
jokes.explanation: Plays well on the established running gag of Chandler's horror at Janice. The escalation to 'end of the world' is proportionate to his well-established dread. Character-specific and rewarding for longtime viewers.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: The baby's probably comfortable in there. It's warm, it's safe... maybe the baby just doesn't want to leave.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Or maybe the baby just doesn't want to come out because you're going to be its father.

jokes.text: Not bad. You know that feeling, trying to blow a Saint Bernard out your ass?
jokes.setup: Someone asks Rachel how she's doing during 21 hours of labor
jokes.punchline: Rachel's grotesque, deadpan simile for labor pain
jokes.explanation: A genuinely surprising image. The Saint Bernard specificity is what elevates it above a generic labor joke — it's not just 'big dog,' it's the most undignified large dog. Strong originality and economy. Gets a big laugh from the unexpectedness of the image.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Get me an epidural! Now!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Rachel, we're not at the hospital yet!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I don't care! I need drugs!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I might have something in my apartment...

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah! We could all just smoke her out!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, that is NOT helping!

jokes.text: Chandler's reaction to hearing Janice — 'Mother of God, it's true!'
jokes.setup: Someone asks if that's Janice they hear
jokes.punchline: Chandler's genuinely horrified confirmation — treating Janice's arrival like a supernatural visitation
jokes.explanation: Functional running-gag execution. 'Mother of God' as a religious invocation for Janice's arrival is a fun choice. Not novel but delivers on audience expectation.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Oh. My. God. I'm dilating faster than you!

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: I win! I win! My baby's coming first!

jokes.text: Oh, this should be easy. I have a very wide pelvis. You remember, Chandler.
jokes.setup: Janice announces she's in labor and that it'll be easy
jokes.punchline: She reminds Chandler of her wide pelvis from their sexual past — in front of everyone, while in labor
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Janice — oversharing, oblivious to social norms, weaponizing past intimacy with Chandler without malice. The 'You remember, Chandler' tag is the knife twist that makes it land. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Patient/Guy
dialogue.line: There was a man in my room last night. A doctor. I saw him clear as day.

dialogue.speaker: Nurse
dialogue.line: Honey, that's the pain medication talking.

jokes.text: It's you. This is yours. / Look how nervous he gets! We haven't slept together in years!
jokes.setup: Janice points at Chandler and says 'It's you. This is yours.' — implying he fathered her child
jokes.punchline: She reveals she was pointing at the room assignment form, laughing at his panic
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection well executed. The setup is genuinely alarming (even if the audience suspects the trick), and the reveal is immediately followed by Janice mocking Chandler's reaction. The two-part payoff — the misdirect AND the humiliation of Chandler — makes it structurally stronger than a simple fake-out.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! Are you saying I'm a bad actor?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I've been on Days of Our Lives! I've won a Daytime Emmy... okay, I didn't win it, but I was in the room when someone won it!

jokes.text: That's funny. Does it hurt? Does the labor hurt?
jokes.setup: Janice has just laughed at Chandler's panic and embarrassment
jokes.punchline: Chandler, flustered and wanting revenge, asks if labor hurts — a transparently petty retaliation disguised as a question
jokes.explanation: Chandler's petty passive-aggression is well-deployed here. The joke works because his wounded pride is so evident. 'Does it hurt?' is satisfyingly childish for a grown man trying to get back at an ex.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, I'm trying to help you out here, man. I'm sharing something personal.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? What are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I once dated a woman with a wooden leg. Her name was Gina. She was a dancer.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Joey, that's—

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No wait, I'm not done. The point is, you gotta put yourself out there. You can't be picky about these things.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm not picky, I just... I don't think that's the same thing.

jokes.text: If you had to, which would you eat? A Seeing Eye dog or a talking gorilla?
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to distract Rachel during labor contractions with a hypothetical game
jokes.punchline: The hypothetical is comically inappropriate — both options are morally horrifying — delivered with cheerful Ross obliviousness
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: the absurdity of the hypothetical itself, and the absurdity of Ross choosing THIS moment to play a game. Both are very Ross. The options are well-chosen — both morally transgressive in different ways.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What else you got?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I have a phobia of cotton balls.

jokes.text: I'd have to say the talking gorilla. 'Cause at least I could explain to him that you're making me eat him.
jokes.setup: Ross asked which Rachel would eat if forced to: a Seeing Eye dog or a talking gorilla
jokes.punchline: Rachel's answer is logically reasoned within the absurd premise, escalating rather than rejecting it
jokes.explanation: Genuinely clever. Rather than refusing the absurd premise, Rachel engages with its internal logic and finds a compassionate loophole — she'd choose the one she could apologize to. The joke is both funny AND reveals character (Rachel's social-anxiety-driven need to be liked, even by a gorilla she's about to eat).

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Okay, so I'm reading this list of shocking revelations, right? And it starts off bad... then it gets worse... and worse... and THEN—

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I find out that Rachel actually DID get off the plane!

jokes.text: Oh. Somebody went to college. / Yeah.
jokes.setup: Rachel gives an impressively reasoned answer to the gorilla hypothetical
jokes.punchline: Ross's mock-impressed 'Somebody went to college' — sarcastic since they both did, but acknowledging her logic was sharper than expected
jokes.explanation: A mild laugh that wraps up the hypothetical game bit. The line is functional but not especially sharp. 'Somebody went to college' is a common enough expression that it doesn't feel particularly fresh.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Joey, this isn't helping. You've just described every guy in New York.

jokes.text: I usually get to know a girl better before I let her spoon me.
jokes.setup: A nurse is spooning Rachel's foot (curling around it to scratch) in a weirdly intimate position
jokes.punchline: Rachel uses 'spoon' in the sexual/cuddling sense rather than the literal position, implying inappropriate intimacy with the nurse
jokes.explanation: Clean wordplay with good structure. The dual meaning of 'spoon' works because the physical position genuinely resembles the intimate act. Sets up the superior 'forking' callback.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, I know what you mean. I hardly ever feel an instant connection with someone.

jokes.text: Relax. It's not like we're forking.
jokes.setup: Rachel has just said 'I usually get to know a girl better before I let her spoon me'
jokes.punchline: 'Forking' as a near-homophone for a profanity, escalating the spoon/fork cutlery/intimacy double entendre
jokes.explanation: The best wordplay in the episode. 'Forking' is a genuinely clever extension of the cutlery double entendre — it escalates the previous joke AND functions as a near-profanity. The economy is nearly perfect (three words). Highly quotable precisely because it's so compact and clean.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: Oh my God!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What?! What is it?!

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: I've never seen anything like this before.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What?! Is the baby okay?!

jokes.text: Oh, that's five, Ross. Five women have had five babies and I have had no babies. Why doesn't she want to come out?
jokes.setup: Rachel has been in labor for over 21 hours while other women in the ward keep delivering
jokes.punchline: Rachel's self-pity and competitive framing — she's essentially losing a race she didn't sign up for, and she's counting
jokes.explanation: Very Rachel — she's keeping score of other women's labors and feeling like a loser. The specificity of 'five women, five babies' makes it funnier than a vague complaint. Character integration is high.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: The baby is breech.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Breech? What does that mean?

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: The buttocks are coming out first.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh, thank God! I thought you were going to say it had my mother's personality.

jokes.text: I think you made such a nice home for her the last nine months that she just doesn't want to leave.
jokes.setup: Rachel is frustrated the baby won't come; Ross tries to comfort her
jokes.punchline: Ross's absurdly optimistic reframe — attributing the baby's delay to the quality of Rachel's uterus as real estate
jokes.explanation: Sweet and funny. The real estate metaphor applied to a womb is unexpected and reveals Ross's desperate need to manage Rachel's feelings. Earns warmth as well as laughs.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Is there any way someone else can just... finish this for me?

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: I'm afraid that's not how it works.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: What if we just... called Monica? She's good at everything!

jokes.text: Oh, look at you making up crap for me.
jokes.setup: Ross has just given his sweet 'nice home' explanation for the baby not coming
jokes.punchline: Rachel immediately sees through it and appreciates the gesture without pretending to believe it
jokes.explanation: A charming button on the exchange. It's funny because it's both grateful and totally undeceived — Rachel's affectionate cynicism is very true to her character.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Thanks for the major ordeal of birth.

jokes.text: Get me drugs, or you light a fire up in there and just smoke it out!
jokes.setup: Rachel has been in labor 21 hours and is at her limit
jokes.punchline: The 'smoke it out' image — treating the birth canal like a pest infestation being fumigated
jokes.explanation: The pest-control metaphor for childbirth is a fresh and somewhat shocking image. 'Smoke it out' earns its laugh through the grotesque specificity of the visual it creates. Good escalation from 'get me drugs' (normal) to 'light a fire up in there' (absurd).

dialogue.speaker: Nurse
dialogue.line: Baby Girl Greene

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Actually, it should be Greene-Geller. Or Geller-Greene. I'm not picky about the order, but my name does need to be in there.

jokes.text: Beat you, sucker! Oh, baby.
jokes.setup: Rachel is finally being taken to the delivery room after 21 hours; she passes another laboring woman in the hall
jokes.punchline: Rachel trash-talks the other patient — turning childbirth into a competition she's winning
jokes.explanation: Perfect callback payoff to the 'five women, five babies' running complaint. Rachel's competitive nature, established throughout the episode, reaches its natural conclusion. 'Beat you, sucker!' from a woman in labor is a memorable, well-earned laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, he's so beautiful. Look at his little fingers. Look at his little toes.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, he's perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I can't believe he's ours.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I know. Although, I gotta say, for something we made with no effort whatsoever, he's pretty great.

jokes.text: Oh, my God! That's the doctor who was in my room before! / Oh. Okay, Mr. Percocet.
jokes.setup: A male patient claims he saw a TV show character (Joey as Dr. Drake Ramoray) in his room asking weird questions
jokes.punchline: He's dismissed as drugged up — 'Mr. Percocet' — ironically, he's completely correct
jokes.explanation: The irony is sharp — the patient is telling the absolute truth and being gaslighted. 'Mr. Percocet' is a clean, economical dismissal. Good callback structure.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I mean, do you realize I was in labor for 19 hours?

jokes.text: I sent my friend Joey in here to find out stuff about you. If it, you know, helps, you came off great. A lot better than I'm coming off right now.
jokes.setup: Ross confesses to the man that Joey was a spy
jokes.punchline: He tries to soften the confession by saying the man 'came off great' — which inadvertently makes Ross look even worse
jokes.explanation: Ross's social obliviousness is perfectly rendered. His attempt to manage the situation only deepens the hole. 'A lot better than I'm coming off right now' is a nice self-aware button that shows some growth while still being maximally awkward.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, is this real? Can I touch it? Oh wow, it's so soft. And warm! Is it supposed to be this warm? That's so weird.

jokes.text: Fake? Excuse me? Hello?
jokes.setup: The man calls Joey a 'fake doctor'
jokes.punchline: Joey is genuinely offended on behalf of his soap opera character, Dr. Drake Ramoray — treating a fictional TV role as a real medical credential
jokes.explanation: One of the best Joey jokes in the episode. His indignation at being called a 'fake doctor' when he is a very real TV doctor is perfectly Joey — he cannot distinguish between playing a character and being one. High character integration, well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, what a beautiful baby! So precious and perfect. I could just... squeeze you to death!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: But I won't. I won't do that.

jokes.text: She was married to a gay ice dancer. She gave birth to her brother's triplets. Her twin sister used to do porn.
jokes.setup: Joey suggests that sharing embarrassing personal info about their friend might help convince the man to give them a second chance
jokes.punchline: Three rapid-fire revelations about Phoebe, each more outrageous than the last — a greatest-hits of Phoebe's backstory played as social currency
jokes.explanation: A wonderfully efficient three-beat escalation. Each item is a callback to established Phoebe lore, and their use as leverage is absurdly logical in Joey's mind. The structure is excellent — three revelations with mounting absurdity, delivered rapidly for comedic rhythm. A satisfying fanservice laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It's normal to cry after giving birth!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I'm not crying because of hormones... I can't find my slippers.

jokes.text: We're trying to dial down the crazy.
jokes.setup: Joey has just listed Phoebe's bizarre life history to a stranger
jokes.punchline: Ross's desperate interjection acknowledges this is backfiring
jokes.explanation: A clean, economical button on joke 26. 'Dial down the crazy' is an efficient three-word acknowledgment that things have gone off the rails. Gets a solid laugh as the deflation beat.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wait, you're not actually naming her 'Baby Girl'?

jokes.text: Don't say 'Oh, my God!' What?! / The baby's buttocks. She's breech. / I thought she had two heads.
jokes.setup: During delivery the doctor reacts with an alarmed 'Oh my God' and then says 'What is that?'
jokes.punchline: It's the baby's bottom (breech birth). Ross, panicking, thought it was two heads — which somehow felt plausible in his terror
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection in a tense scene. The doctor's alarm creates genuine dread, the 'buttocks' resolution is funny in its mundanity, and Ross's 'two heads' is an absurd escalation that lands well because his panic is total. Provides comedy relief at a dramatically tense moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: We're going to name her Isabella.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No. No, that's not her vibe at all.

jokes.text: You have no idea how much this hurts.
jokes.setup: During a grueling delivery, Ross asks if Rachel is okay
jokes.punchline: Rachel's quiet, exhausted understatement — the calm is funnier than screaming at this point
jokes.explanation: A mild laugh through understatement at an extreme moment. Functional but not especially crafted — the humor is entirely situational.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Delilah? That's the woman who cut off Samson's hair and betrayed him to the Philistines. That's not a name, that's a cautionary tale.

jokes.text: Oh, thanks for coming out of me.
jokes.setup: Rachel holds her newborn daughter for the first time
jokes.punchline: Instead of a sweeping declaration of love, she thanks the baby matter-of-factly for finally arriving — like thanking a houseguest who overstayed
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest jokes. It earns its laugh by subverting every expectation of a birth scene — the overwhelming emotion is replaced by polite gratitude, like a thank-you note. 'Coming out of me' is simultaneously clinical and affectionate. Excellent economy (six words), high originality, and genuinely earned because it comes after 21+ hours of labor. This line also lands emotionally, which makes it exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I've had names picked out since I was 14.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Let me guess... Pizza? Nacho? Meatball?

jokes.text: Oh, no. Baby Girl Geller-Greene.
jokes.setup: The hospital has assigned the baby the name 'Baby Girl Greene' — using only Rachel's last name
jokes.punchline: Ross quietly but firmly insists on hyphenating — asserting paternity in the gentlest possible way
jokes.explanation: A quiet character moment with a good laugh. Ross's dignity in asserting himself without drama is both funny and sweet. Works better in context of his usual over-earnestness.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We're naming her Emma.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Emma? Really? That's the name of every other baby in New York right now.

jokes.text: Oh, I'm so glad you guys got drunk and had sex.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is holding the baby and expressing her joy at the birth
jokes.punchline: Instead of a sentimental compliment about love or fate, she cuts to the blunt mechanics of how the baby was conceived
jokes.explanation: Classic Phoebe — cutting through sentiment with accidental bluntness. The joke works because it's both true (they did get drunk and have sex) and completely wrong for the tender moment. High quotability because it's a universal sentiment that most people would have suppressed.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, Emma Geller sounds nice, but Emma Bing sounds like a sound effect.

jokes.text: It's incredible. One minute she's inside you, and then 47 hours later, here she is.
jokes.setup: Ross is marveling at the miracle of birth
jokes.punchline: '47 hours later' inadvertently reminds everyone how absurdly long the labor was, undercutting the wonder
jokes.explanation: Ross's obliviousness is well-deployed — he's trying to express wonder but just re-opens the wound. The specific '47 hours' makes it funnier than a round number.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: This is my son, Chandler Jr.

dialogue.speaker: Other Character
dialogue.line: He's beautiful, Janice.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: I know! And he's already engaged. I've arranged a marriage with Monica and Chandler's baby. Isn't that wonderful?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, what? We haven't even decided on a name yet!

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Oh, it's all settled. I've had my lawyer draw up the prenup. The wedding will be at The Plaza in the fall of 2027.

jokes.text: She looks so real.
jokes.setup: Everyone is admiring the newborn
jokes.punchline: Phoebe says 'she looks so real' — implying she expected the baby to look fake, or that reality itself is a surprise
jokes.explanation: Perfect Phoebe line. Only Phoebe would be surprised that a real baby looks real. Four words, maximally efficient, completely character-specific. The 'you know what I mean' follow-up adds to it because she doesn't explain and probably couldn't.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: What happens when Ross remarries?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: We'll just have to get divorced again.

jokes.text: Oh, I could squeeze your little head. I won't.
jokes.setup: Phoebe is holding the baby and cooing over how cute she is
jokes.punchline: 'I could squeeze your little head' sounds threatening; the reassuring 'I won't' makes it funnier by acknowledging the dark reading
jokes.explanation: Very economical dark comedy. The beat rests on the ambiguity of 'squeeze your head' (affectionate vs. violent) and then punctures it with the deadpan reassurance. 'I won't' does enormous comedy work in two syllables.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: My ex-husband's new girlfriend? She's nothing but a gold-digging tramp who couldn't tell a Hermès bag from a garbage bag!

jokes.text: You guys are all sleep-deprived. I don't see you weeping because you put your slippers on the wrong feet.
jokes.setup: Monica is crying inexplicably; the doctor says it's normal and they're sleep-deprived
jokes.punchline: Rachel uses a specific, absurd detail — wrong-footed slippers — to illustrate Monica's broken state
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'slippers on the wrong feet' is what makes this work — it's the right level of mundane absurdity to illustrate sleep-deprivation comedy. Calls out Monica's state in a way that gets a laugh from the visual image.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh, wow. She's... she's beautiful. She has your eyes.

dialogue.speaker: Janice
dialogue.line: Thank you!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: And... and she has your nose.

jokes.text: Wait, it's not gonna be Baby Girl? I thought that was so original.
jokes.setup: Ross and Rachel are about to reveal the baby's real name
jokes.punchline: Phoebe genuinely thought 'Baby Girl' was an intentional, creative name choice — not a placeholder
jokes.explanation: Very Phoebe — she's always a beat behind on social norms and genuinely thought 'Baby Girl' was edgy and original. Well-timed and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, you forgot the sodas.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know, I know, I was talking to that nurse and I just...

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, one day you're gonna be performing surgery and someone's gonna sneeze and you're not gonna notice because you're too busy flirting with some cute anesthesiologist.

jokes.text: Oh, great! At least she sounds like a biblical whore.
jokes.setup: Ross says the baby doesn't feel like an 'Isabella.' Rachel offers the alternative name 'Delilah.'
jokes.punchline: Phoebe's pseudo-consolation that at least 'Delilah' has biblical whorish credibility — a backhanded compliment at best
jokes.explanation: Genuinely surprising. The specificity of 'biblical whore' (not just 'whore', not just 'biblical') shows real craft in the word choice. Phoebe's oblivious attempt to find the silver lining is perfect, and the line is quotable precisely because it's delivered as comfort. One of the episode's funniest Phoebe moments.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I can't decide who Emma looks like.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, she has your eyes.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, those are Rachel's.

jokes.text: Oh, no, it's gonna be named after some snack or baked good, isn't it?
jokes.setup: Phoebe mentions she has baby names picked out since she was 14
jokes.punchline: Ross preemptively fears she'll name a child after a food — a reasonable concern given Phoebe's history of eccentric choices
jokes.explanation: A good setup for the name reveal. Ross's worry about Phoebe's taste is very grounded in what we know about the character. Functions well as anticipatory comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: But she's only twenty-four!

jokes.text: See, I don't want it. [after a beat of considering 'Emma']
jokes.setup: Phoebe just said they'd never want the name 'Emma' for their own children
jokes.punchline: After a noticeable pause where she clearly considers it, she insists she doesn't want it
jokes.explanation: The beat works because the pause tells us everything — she does want it. The delivery-dependent laugh is classic sitcom timing.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Whoa! Whoa! Whoa! That's not fair! How come she gets two?!

jokes.text: Yeah. But I love you more. Besides, nothing goes with Bing. So I'm screwed.
jokes.setup: Monica has given up her beloved baby name 'Emma' so Ross and Rachel can use it
jokes.punchline: Chandler's sweet acknowledgment that Monica loves Ross and Rachel more than the name, then immediately deflates it with the practical problem: nothing rhymes well with 'Bing'
jokes.explanation: One of Chandler's best moments in the episode. The structure is perfect: genuine sweetness, then self-deprecating pivot to 'Bing' as an impossible surname for any name. High character integration — Chandler has always been defined by his absurd surname, and this is a clever way to weaponize it. The 'So I'm screwed' button is excellent economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I mean, come on, Ross. You're not even sure about us yet.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What? Of course I'm sure about us!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Well, you know what? Your future wife—or whatever—is gonna hate me anyway.

jokes.text: Aaron Lipman-Guralnick would like to say hello to his future bride.
jokes.setup: Janice arrives to meet the new baby with her own newborn
jokes.punchline: Janice has already arranged her hours-old son's marriage to the also-hours-old Emma
jokes.explanation: Very Janice — impulsive, over-the-top, completely oblivious to appropriateness. The hyphenated surname 'Lipman-Guralnick' is a funny detail suggesting the father is also Jewish (a Janice type). The speed of her matchmaking (the baby is hours old) is well-deployed.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So we're really doing this? We're going to try to have a baby?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, I think so. I mean, unless you've changed your mind?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: No, no, I haven't. It's just... remember when we found out we couldn't have kids naturally, and we got all romantic in the hospital? Well, turns out that was the most fertile I've been in years.

jokes.text: Wow, he kind of takes your breath away, doesn't he?
jokes.setup: Everyone looks at Janice's newborn son Aaron
jokes.punchline: Chandler's loaded compliment — implying the baby is so notably unusual (or large-nosed) that it's genuinely stunning
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom backhanded compliment. Works because Chandler's tortured politeness is so recognizable, and the audience is primed to expect Janice's child to be as overwhelming as she is.

jokes.text: Well, then he gets a divorce. It's Ross.
jokes.setup: Janice suggests Rachel's situation will fall apart when Ross meets someone else and starts his 'real family'
jokes.punchline: Rachel's breezy reply — his marriages never last anyway, so the threat is hollow
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — three words do the work of a whole speech. The joke lands because it's both a callback to Ross's established history and a genuine character insight (Rachel isn't particularly threatened because she knows his track record). One of the most quotable lines in the episode.

jokes.text: I'm lucky if my kid gets to spend a weekend with her father and little Miss New Boobs.
jokes.setup: Janice is warning Rachel that fathers drift away
jokes.punchline: 'Little Miss New Boobs' as the nickname for her ex's new girlfriend — bitter, petty, hilariously specific
jokes.explanation: Very funny line. Janice's bitterness finds its perfect expression in this nickname. 'Miss New Boobs' is petty in a very specific, recognizable way — it's not 'the younger woman' or 'that woman,' it's hyper-focused on one physical feature. Highly quotable. Works as both a Janice character moment and an incisive joke.

jokes.text: Man, you see the kid on that nose?
jokes.setup: Janice has left; Chandler and Monica are looking at Aaron
jokes.punchline: Chandler finally says what everyone was thinking — the baby has a very large nose (like Janice)
jokes.explanation: A reliable cheap shot that nonetheless works because it's held until after Janice has left — the timing is the joke. The slight grammatical oddness of 'the kid on that nose' adds to the delivery. Not high craft, but functional.

jokes.text: Right. / We don't want to go down that road. / No. That's why I brought it up.
jokes.setup: Ross says they can't let the kiss happen again and they don't want to go down that road
jokes.punchline: Rachel's 'That's why I brought it up' — pointed sarcasm acknowledging that you don't bring things up to avoid them
jokes.explanation: Economical and sharp. Rachel's sarcasm perfectly exposes Ross's self-delusion — if he truly didn't want to go down that road, he wouldn't have brought it up. The joke is structurally sound and character-specific.

jokes.text: They didn't have any sodas? / Oh, my God, I'm sorry. I was talking to this nurse. Completely forgot. / And so it begins.
jokes.setup: Ross went to get Rachel a soda and came back empty-handed, distracted by talking to a nurse
jokes.punchline: Joey's ominous 'And so it begins' — confirming Janice's prophecy that Ross would be distracted by other women almost immediately
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest structural jokes. It works as an immediate callback to Janice's warning AND it's Joey — the most loyal, least cynical character — delivering the punchline. The irony is rich: Janice's dark prophecy comes true within five minutes of her saying it, and even Joey sees it. Excellent economy with 'And so it begins.'

jokes.text: Oh, what, are you kidding? She's gorgeous! It's all Rachel.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Joey are watching baby Emma through the hospital window
jokes.punchline: Chandler enthusiastically credits all of Emma's good looks to Rachel — implicitly saying she looks nothing like Ross, which is a dig at Ross delivered as a compliment
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed implied insult. The joke lives in what Chandler doesn't say. Good character integration — Chandler's backhanded compliments are a signature move.

jokes.text: I'm sorry. For the last time, why aren't you two together again? No, I know. Because you're not in that place. Which would be fine, except you totally are.
jokes.setup: Joey is watching Ross watch Rachel through the window
jokes.punchline: Joey cuts through Ross's self-deception with unusual perceptiveness — 'except you totally are' in that place
jokes.explanation: Joey is at his best when he's accidentally wise. The joke works because Joey — often the least perceptive character — sees exactly what's happening, while Ross is oblivious. The 'except you totally are' construction is satisfying.

jokes.text: Hey. I saw a woman breastfeeding twins at the same time. It is like a freak show up here.
jokes.setup: Joey returns from wandering the maternity ward
jokes.punchline: Joey's report of the maternity ward as a 'freak show' — his reference point for unusual human spectacle
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey — his frame of reference for awe is a carnival sideshow. The joke is functional and in-character, though not particularly crafted.

jokes.text: Please. He'll be with his real family. The twins and little Miss New Boobs.
jokes.setup: Rachel is worrying about being alone; Monica mentions Ross
jokes.punchline: Rachel has completely internalized Janice's framing — including the 'little Miss New Boobs' nickname, now adopting it as her own
jokes.explanation: A beautifully ironic callback — Rachel has now adopted Janice's exact phrasing, suggesting Janice's poison has seeped in despite her dismissal. The joke is structurally strong because it rewards attentive viewers and shows the emotional contagion of Janice's warning.

jokes.text: Okay, how long was I watching that woman?
jokes.setup: Joey returns to find Rachel upset, and realizes he's been gone too long watching the breastfeeding twins
jokes.punchline: Joey's self-aware acknowledgment that he lost track of time voyeuristically watching a nursing mother — with no guilt, just curiosity about how long
jokes.explanation: Good callback. Joey's question is funny because he's not asking out of shame — he's genuinely curious about the duration. Very true to his character. The understated delivery is what makes it land.

jokes.text: Oh, my God! / Joey? / Oh, my God.
jokes.setup: Joey is reaching under Ross's coat to retrieve tissues; the camera lingers uncomfortably
jokes.punchline: What appears to be a compromising moment (Joey seems to be groping Rachel's lower half, as Ross's coat is covering the area) plays out in a prolonged, silent reaction — both characters mortified
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed physical comedy bit dependent on staging. The long pause and the double 'Oh, my God' play out the visual joke before dialogue resolves it. The comedy lives in the uncomfortable gap — a pure visual gag with almost no dialogue. High rewatch value because viewers look for the staging.

jokes.text: That was amazing. / I know. / Hey, do you realize that we may have just changed our lives forever? We may have started our family.
jokes.setup: Chandler and Monica emerge from their hospital room tryst, speaking with the gravity of a momentous decision
jokes.punchline: The grand language ('changed our lives forever,' 'started our family') applies to what was essentially a quickie in a hospital storage room
jokes.explanation: A satisfying wrap-up to the Monica/Chandler hospital sex subplot. The joke works through tonal disparity — epic language for an impulsive decision made in a broom closet. Not the sharpest payoff but well-structured as an episode button.

jokes.text: And if not, we got to do it on a bucket.
jokes.setup: Chandler is waxing poetic about possibly having conceived their family
jokes.punchline: He adds a matter-of-fact silver lining — if the conception didn't work, at least the act itself was novel (on/near a bucket)
jokes.explanation: A perfect episode-closing joke. Chandler deflates Monica's romantic moment with a deadpan detail about a bucket — maximally undignified, maximally economical. 'On a bucket' is a great final image for the episode's comedic subplot. The best Chandler joke of the episode and a strong final beat.

insight: Season finale trades laughs for emotion—41 jokes spread thin across 24 minutes.
